observation_summary: The command-line parser fails to correctly merge user-provided arguments with default values when the number of provided arguments is less than the maximum allowed. Specifically, if a user provides one argument when two are allowed, the system ignores the remaining default values instead of appending them.
hypothesis: The argument processing logic in the parser incorrectly treats the presence of any user-provided arguments as a signal to ignore all default values, rather than filling the remaining slots up to the maximum allowed count.
prediction: The code responsible for merging user arguments and default values likely contains a conditional check that skips default value processing entirely if the user-provided argument list is not empty.
experiment_rationale: The failure occurs during the argument parsing phase where the command-line object is populated. The test cases demonstrate that the parser correctly handles the 'all defaults' case and the 'all user-provided' case, but fails the 'partial' case, indicating a flaw in the logic that combines these two sources of values.
reasoning_summary: The issue is a procedural logic error in how the parser handles the combination of user-provided arguments and default values. It is not a missing guard (Checking) or a simple wrong constant (Assignment/Initialization), but a flaw in the algorithmic strategy for populating the argument list when partial input is provided. This fits the Algorithm/Method definition of a procedure that requires correction in its computational strategy.
evidence_used: Bug report description: 'When using multple arguments and defaults, the behaviour is counter-intuitive and will only pick up a default if no args are passed in.'

alternative_types.why_not_primary: While there is a conditional check involved, the root cause is the logic of the argument merging procedure itself, not just a missing validation guard.
The capability exists, but the implementation of the argument merging algorithm is flawed; it does not require a design-level change.
